messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 80
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 64

He keeps the photograph tucked inside the drawer of his nightstand—not hidden, but not displayed. It shows a younger version of himself, still in his Coast Guard uniform, standing beside a man whose name he cannot say aloud. The other man is smiling, one arm draped around Raj’s shoulders, both of them squinting into the morning sun off the coast of Mumbai. Raj is eighty now, and for fifty-three years he has not spoken that man’s name to anyone. Not to his wife, before she passed. Not to his sons, who visit once a month and leave when he grows quiet. Not to the old friends who still call from the veterans’ association—calls he never answers.

The event happened in a single, unforgiving instant. He was thirty-two, a petty officer second class on a search-and-rescue cutter. The seas were rough—monsoon season, the Arabian Sea churning gray and angry. A fishing trawler had sent a distress signal, and his crew was attempting a winch transfer of a stranded fisherman. Raj was on the deck, steadying the line. The cable snapped. He remembers the sound—a whip crack, then a wet thud. The snapped end caught his crewmate across the face, and before Raj could move, the man was on the deck, blood seeping between his fingers. Raj knew first aid. He applied pressure, shouted for the medic. But the injury was severe. The man lost an eye and suffered a traumatic brain injury. He never returned to duty. And Raj carried the certainty that he had pulled the line too hard, that his grip had been off by half a second.

Now, in the small apartment in New Jersey where he moved after his wife’s death, Raj lives inside a loop of that moment. It comes without warning. The sound of a pressure cooker’s hiss becomes the hiss of the cable. A heavy door slamming becomes the thud. He flinches when someone touches his shoulder from behind. He has not stepped onto a boat in forty years, not even a ferry. He tells his sons he gets seasick. The truth is, he cannot bear the feel of a deck under his feet—the instability, the memory of that lurch when the cable went taut and then slack.

His days are structured, deliberate. He wakes at five, makes tea in the same blue mug, sits by the window. He avoids news about the coast guard or the navy. He turned off the television during a documentary about maritime rescues, then sat in the dark for an hour, trembling. At night, he sleeps only two or three hours at a stretch. His dreams are not vivid, but they are repetitive—he is always holding a line, and someone is waiting for him to pull correctly, and he can never do it right.

His sons have noticed. They ask if he is sleeping, if he is eating. He says yes to both. But he has lost weight. The corner store clerk, who is also South Asian, greets him in Hindi, and Raj responds in English, as though to keep distance. He does not want to talk about the old country, the old life. He wants only to sit in the quiet and wait for the day to pass.

Today, like every day, he opens the drawer and looks at the photograph. He does not take it out. He runs his thumb along the edge of the frame, then closes the drawer. He goes to the window. The street is empty. Somewhere, a car door slams. He flinches. And he waits.
